samples.text:
The table shows how much energy people use in six countries in 2023 and what percentage of this energy come from renewable sources, and also how much the renewable share changed since 2013.

Canada used the most energy per person with 350 GJ, and Saudi Arabia was second with 310 GJ. Australia and Norway used 225 GJ and 210 GJ. France used less, 145 GJ, and Brazil used only 60 GJ, which is the lowest.

For renewable energy, Norway had the highest share with 61%, and Brazil was also high with 49%. Canada was 29%. However, Australia and France had quite low shares, 14% and 16%, and Saudi Arabia had only 1%, that is very low.

All the countries increased their renewable share since 2013. Norway increase the most by 9 points, and Brazil by 8 points and Australia by 7 points. France went up 5 points, Canada 3 points and Saudi Arabia only 1 point.

Overall, the countries which use a lot of energy does not always have a high renewable share, for example Saudi Arabia.
samples.why: All three columns reported accurately · overview present but late and underdeveloped · each column described separately with repetitive verbs (used, had) · agreement and tense errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The table provides information about energy consumption per person in six countries in 2023, along with the renewable share and how this changed over the previous decade.

Overall, energy use varied widely between the countries, and there was no clear link between the amount consumed and the renewable share. Norway and Brazil relied most heavily on renewables, while all six countries increased their renewable share since 2013.

Canada was the largest consumer of energy, at 350 GJ per person, followed by Saudi Arabia at 310 GJ. Australia and Norway had similar levels of consumption, at 225 GJ and 210 GJ respectively, while France used 145 GJ. Brazil's figure was by far the lowest, at just 60 GJ, which is less than a fifth of Canada's.

Regarding renewable energy, Norway had the highest share at 61%, after the largest increase of 9 points. Brazil came second with 49%, after an increase of 8 points. Canada's share was 29%, but it grew only 3 points. Australia and France had much lower proportions of 14% and 16%, although both of them improved by 7 and 5 points. Saudi Arabia, despite its high energy use, obtained only 1% from renewable sources and saw the smallest change of 1 point.
samples.why: Clear overview noting the lack of correlation · key features highlighted with useful comparisons · logical paragraphing · some less common vocabulary · mostly error-free, with a tense slip and slightly imprecise pairing.

samples.text:
The table compares six countries in terms of per capita energy consumption in 2023, the share of that energy derived from renewable sources, and the change in this share since 2013.

Two points stand out. First, levels of energy use bear little relation to reliance on renewables: some heavy consumers depend almost entirely on other sources, whereas relatively modest consumers make extensive use of renewable energy. Second, the renewable share rose in every country over the decade, although to very different degrees.

Canada and Saudi Arabia were the heaviest users, consuming 350 GJ and 310 GJ per person respectively, yet their renewable profiles diverged sharply. Canada obtained 29% of its energy from renewable sources, compared with a mere 1% in Saudi Arabia, where the share had grown by only a single point. Australia (225 GJ) and Norway (210 GJ) consumed similar amounts, but Norway's renewable share, at 61%, was more than four times Australia's 14%.

At the lower end of consumption, France used 145 GJ per person and sourced 16% of its energy from renewables. Brazil, whose consumption of 60 GJ was the lowest by a wide margin, had the second-highest renewable share at 49%. It was also, alongside Norway, among the fastest improvers, with gains of 8 and 9 points respectively.
samples.why: Two-part overview captures the key relationships · figures selected and paired skilfully · cohesion and referencing managed well · precise vocabulary (diverged, per capita, a mere) · wide range of accurate structures.
